subject: Mathematics
title: Recipe Scaling for a School Festival
hook: Priya's mother makes a kheer (rice pudding) for 4 people using 1 cup rice, 2 cups milk, 3 tbsp ghee. For 20 people at the school festival, how much of each ingredient? Arjun uses ratios to scale the recipe perfectly.

slides.title: Scaling the Festival Kheer
slides.storyContext: Priya's mother's kheer recipe serves 4 people: 1 cup rice, 2 cups milk, 3 tbsp ghee. The school festival expects 20 people. 'Do I just add more randomly?' she asks. Arjun says: 'No! Scale using ratios. The recipe must stay in the same proportion.'

image.alt: Scaling the Festival Kheer — Proportional Reasoning-1

slides.title: The Festival Challenge
slides.storyContext: Priya and Arjun brainstorm in the kitchen. Priya says: 'If I just double everything, will it work?' Arjun shakes his head: '4 people becomes 20? That's not double, that's five times!' They write it down: 4 × scale factor = 20. Scale factor = 5. Every ingredient gets multiplied by 5—not more, not less.
slides.inSimpleWords: To scale a recipe, find how many times bigger it needs to be.

points.label: Definition
points.text: A ratio compares two quantities. Rice : Milk = 1 : 2 means for every 1 cup rice, use 2 cups milk.

points.label: Notation
points.text: Write as 1:2, 1/2, or '1 to 2'. All mean the same comparison.

points.label: Everyday Examples
points.text: Recipe ratios (1:2), map ratios (1:1000000), probability (3:5 for winning odds).

points.label: Same Ratio, Different Numbers
points.text: 1:2 (1 rice : 2 milk), 2:4 (2 rice : 4 milk), 5:10 (5 rice : 10 milk)—all taste identical.

points.label: Cross-Multiplication Check
points.text: For ratios a:b and c:d, if a×d = b×c, they are equivalent. E.g., 1×4 = 2×2 ✓

points.label: Simplest Form
points.text: Reduce 10:20 by dividing both by 10 → 1:2. Simplest form is clearest.

slides.title: Example 1: Scaling Kheer

example.problem: Scale the kheer recipe for 20 people. Original (4 people): 1 cup rice, 2 cups milk, 3 tbsp ghee.
example.solution: Scale factor = 20÷4 = 5. New recipe: 1×5 = 5 cups rice, 2×5 = 10 cups milk, 3×5 = 15 tbsp ghee.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply all ingredients by the scale factor.

slides.title: Priya Tests the Scaled Recipe
slides.storyContext: They make the festival kheer using the scaled amounts: 5 cups rice, 10 cups milk, 15 tbsp ghee. The first batch feeds exactly 20 people. Priya tastes it: 'It's perfect! The ratio stayed the same, so it tastes just like Amma's small-batch version.'

example.problem: Original recipe serves 4. Half-recipe for 2 people: 1 cup rice, 2 cups milk, 3 tbsp ghee.
example.solution: Scale factor = 2÷4 = 0.5. Divide all: 1×0.5 = 0.5 cup rice, 2×0.5 = 1 cup milk, 3×0.5 = 1.5 tbsp ghee.

points.label: Formula
points.text: Scale factor = New amount ÷ Original amount. For 4 → 20 people: 20÷4 = 5.

points.label: Scaling Up
points.text: If scale factor > 1, recipe grows. If < 1, recipe shrinks.

points.label: Checking Your Work
points.text: Original × scale factor = new. Check: 4×5 = 20 ✓

points.label: Definition
points.text: Two quantities are directly proportional if as one increases, the other increases at the same rate.

points.label: Constant Ratio Test
points.text: If x and y are directly proportional, x:y is always the same. E.g., 1 rice : 2 milk stays 5 rice : 10 milk.

points.label: Formula
points.text: y = kx, where k is the constant of proportionality. E.g., milk = 2 × rice.

slides.title: Arjun Discovers the Pattern
slides.storyContext: At the festival, Arjun writes down quantities for 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 people. He notices: rice is always half the milk amount. No matter the scale, rice:milk stays 1:2. 'This is the constant!' he says. 'The formula is milk = 2 × rice.'

points.label: What is k?
points.text: k is the number you multiply by to go from one quantity to another. For kheer: k = 2 (milk = 2 × rice).

points.label: Finding k
points.text: Divide one quantity by the other: k = y÷x. E.g., 10 cups milk ÷ 5 cups rice = 2.

points.label: Using k
points.text: Once you know k, predict any value: If 30 people, rice = 30÷4 = 7.5 cups, milk = 7.5 × 2 = 15 cups.

example.problem: If 3 notebooks cost Rs 60, what do 7 notebooks cost? (Assuming direct proportion.)
example.solution: Cost per notebook k = 60÷3 = Rs 20. Cost of 7 notebooks = 7×20 = Rs 140.

points.label: Straight Line Through Origin
points.text: Plot people vs. rice cups: (4,1), (8,2), (12,3), (20,5). Points line up through (0,0).

points.label: Slope = Constant k
points.text: Rise÷Run = 1÷4 = 0.25. The slope tells k: rice = 0.25 × people.

points.label: No Recipe = No Ingredients
points.text: At 0 people, 0 rice, 0 milk. Direct proportion always crosses origin.

slides.title: Not Everything Scales Proportionally
slides.storyContext: Later, Arjun asks: 'Does cooking time scale the same way?' Grandpa says no. 'Doubling kheer doesn't double cooking time. Some things are proportional, some aren't. Always check the real world.'

example.problem: A recipe uses 1 cup flour for 4 cookies. Does 2 cups flour make 8 cookies? Oven time also matters.
example.solution: More ingredients ≠ proportionally more cookies if baking time stays same. If you double flour but bake for same time, cookies burn or underbake. Not directly proportional.

example.problem: Original kheer (4 people): 1 cup rice, 2 cups milk, 3 tbsp ghee. If Priya makes it for 10 people, what are the new amounts?
example.solution: Scale factor = 10÷4 = 2.5. Rice: 1×2.5 = 2.5 cups. Milk: 2×2.5 = 5 cups. Ghee: 3×2.5 = 7.5 tbsp.

example.problem: Arjun needs 20 cups milk for the festival. Original recipe has 2 cups milk for 4 people. How many people will this serve?
example.solution: Scale factor = 20÷2 = 10. So original 4 × 10 = 40 people. Check: 4 → 10× scale → 40 people, 2 cups milk → 10× → 20 cups. ✓

example.problem: 10 cups rice to 20 cups milk. Simplify the ratio and find the constant k.
example.solution: 10:20 = 1:2 (divide both by 10). k = 2 (milk = 2 × rice).

points.label: Not Always Direct
points.text: Some quantities are inversely proportional: as one increases, the other decreases. E.g., workers vs. time to finish job.

points.label: Formula Difference
points.text: Direct: y = kx. Inverse: y = k/x (constant divided by x).

points.label: Example
points.text: 10 workers finish job in 5 days. 5 workers finish in 10 days. 50 = 10×5 = 5×10. Constant k = 50.

example.problem: A festival cooking team needs to make 100 kg kheer. 4 cooks take 8 hours. How long for 2 cooks?
example.solution: Inverse: workers × hours = constant. 4×8 = 32. So 2×h = 32. h = 16 hours. Fewer workers = more time.

points.label: Recipes & Cooking
points.text: Scale ingredients by serving size. Direct proportion.

points.label: Maps & Distance
points.text: 1:1000000 scale on map. 1 cm = 1000000 cm (10 km) on ground. Direct proportion.

points.label: Money & Shopping
points.text: Cost = quantity × price/unit. Direct proportion with price constant.

example.problem: A map of Punjab uses scale 1:500000. The distance from Amritsar to Ludhiana on map is 8 cm. What is actual distance?
example.solution: Actual distance = map distance × scale factor. 8 cm × 500000 = 4000000 cm = 40 km.

points.label: Method 1: Constant Ratio
points.text: For each pair, calculate ratio. If all ratios equal, quantities are proportional. 4:2, 8:4, 12:6 all = 2:1 ✓

points.label: Method 2: Cross-Multiply
points.text: For pairs (a,b) and (c,d): if a×d = b×c, they're proportional. 4×4 = 2×8 ✓ (both = 16)

points.label: Method 3: Graph
points.text: Plot points on graph. If they form a straight line through origin, quantities are directly proportional.

slides.title: The Festival Success
slides.storyContext: Festival day arrives. Priya and Arjun serve 100+ guests using their ratio knowledge. Grandpa watches them measure perfectly. 'You both learned that proportions are everywhere—cooking, budgets, maps, everything scales with ratios.'

slides.title: Proportional Reasoning

points.text: Ratios compare quantities; equivalent ratios stay proportional.
Scale factor multiplies or divides all quantities equally.
Direct proportion: y = kx (constant k). Always a straight line through origin.
Not everything scales—always verify with real-world observations.

slides.inSimpleWords: Proportions scale recipes and prices perfectly.

subject: Mathematics
title: Cricket Scores and Batting Averages
hook: Arjun watches an Indian cricket match. The batter has a batting average of 0.75 (three hits in four attempts). Is that the same as ¾? Priya shows him how decimals, fractions, and percentages are all the same number dressed up differently.

slides.title: Fractions in Disguise: Three Forms of One Number
Batting Average Mystery
slides.storyContext: Arjun watches the IPL (Indian Premier League) match on TV. Commentator says: 'Batter's average this season: 0.75.' Arjun wonders: 'Is that good?' Priya says: '0.75 = ¾ = 75%. That means 3 hits out of every 4 attempts. Pretty good for cricket!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Decimals, fractions, and percentages are the same.

image.alt: Batting Average Mystery — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: The Three Disguises
slides.storyContext: Arjun is confused. Priya draws three columns on paper: Fraction (¾), Decimal (0.75), Percentage (75%). 'Same person, three outfits,' she laughs. 'The batter succeeds ¾ of the time, or 0.75 (out of 1.0), or 75% (out of 100). They're triplets, not strangers.'

points.label: Parts and Wholes
points.text: Fraction = numerator (top) ÷ denominator (bottom). ¾ means 3 parts out of 4 equal parts.

points.label: What Denominator Means
points.text: Denominator = how many equal parts the whole is divided into. ¾: the whole is cut into 4 pieces.

points.label: What Numerator Means
points.text: Numerator = how many of those pieces you have. ¾: you have 3 of the 4 pieces.

points.label: The Conversion
points.text: Divide numerator by denominator. ¾ = 3÷4 = 0.75

points.label: Long Division Method
points.text: ⅝: 5÷8 = 0.625. Put decimal, divide: 50÷8=6 rem 2, 20÷8=2 rem 4, 40÷8=5. Result: 0.625.

points.label: Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths
points.text: 0.75: 7 in tenths place (0.7), 5 in hundredths place (0.05). 0.75 = 0.7 + 0.05.

points.label: Reading Decimals
points.text: 0.75 is 'zero point seven five' or 'seventy-five hundredths'. Think of it as a fraction: 75/100.

points.label: Decimal to Fraction
points.text: 0.75 = 75/100. Then simplify using GCD: 75/100 = ¾.

example.problem: A cricketer hits 5 fours in 8 deliveries. Express as fraction, decimal, and percentage.
example.solution: Fraction: ⅝. Decimal: 5÷8 = 0.625. Percentage: 0.625 × 100 = 62.5%. All three express the same batting success.

image.alt: Example 1: Cricket Batting Average — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: Arjun Checks His Cricket Stats
slides.storyContext: Arjun looks at his own practice stats: 6 successful runs out of 10. Priya helps: '6/10 = 0.6 = 60%. You're 60% successful. If you practice more, can you hit 75% like the pro?'

points.label: Percent Means Hundredths
points.text: 'Per cent' = per hundred. 75% = 75/100 = 0.75.

points.label: Converting Decimal to Percent
points.text: Multiply by 100: 0.75 × 100 = 75%. Or move decimal 2 places right: 0.75 → 75.

points.label: Converting Percent to Decimal
points.text: Divide by 100: 75% ÷ 100 = 0.75. Or move decimal 2 places left: 75 → 0.75.

points.label: Step 1: Count Decimal Places
points.text: 0.75 has 2 decimal places → put over 100. 0.625 has 3 decimal places → put over 1000.

points.label: Prime Factorization
points.text: 75 = 3×5². 100 = 2²×5². Common factors: 5². So GCD = 5×5 = 25.

points.label: Then Simplify
points.text: Divide both numerator and denominator by GCD: 75÷25=3, 100÷25=4. Result: ¾.

example.problem: Express 40% as a fraction in simplest form.

image.alt: Example 2: Percentage to Fraction — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: Simplifying Arjun's Stats
slides.storyContext: Arjun's average: 20 hits in 80 attempts. Priya simplifies: '20/80 = 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%. Easier to remember—you're 25% successful. Work on your technique!'

points.label: What They Are
points.text: Some fractions give non-ending decimals. ⅓ = 0.333... (3 repeats forever).

points.label: Notation
points.text: Write a bar over repeating digits: 0.3̄ (means 0.333...), 0.16̄ (means 0.1666...).

points.label: Which Fractions Repeat?
points.text: Denominators 3,6,7,9,11... give repeating. Denominators 2,4,5,10... give terminating (ending).

example.problem: Convert 0.333... (repeating) to a fraction.
example.solution: 0.333... = ⅓. Check: 1÷3 = 0.333... ✓. Decimals that repeat often hide fractions with 3,6,7,9 in denominator.

points.label: Marking Key Points
points.text: 0, ¼ (0.25), ½ (0.5), ¾ (0.75), 1 equally spaced on a line.

points.label: Ordering Numbers
points.text: 0.6 = ⅗ lies between ½ (0.5) and ¾ (0.75). Helps compare and order values.

points.label: Mixed Numbers
points.text: 1¼ = 1.25, 1⅖ = 1.4. Improper fraction 7/5 = 1.4 on the line.

example.problem: A batsman scores 3 centuries in 12 matches. Write as fraction, decimal, and percentage.
example.solution: Fraction: 3/12 = ¼ (simplified). Decimal: 0.25. Percentage: 25%.

example.problem: Order from smallest to largest: 0.6, ⅗, 62%, 0.602
example.solution: Convert all to decimals: 0.6, 0.6, 0.62, 0.602. Order: ⅗ and 0.6 (tied), 0.602, then 0.62 (largest).

example.problem: Simplify 30/45 and convert to decimal and percent.
example.solution: GCD(30,45)=15. Simplify: 30÷15=2, 45÷15=3. So 30/45 = ⅔. Decimal: 2÷3 = 0.666... Percent: 66.67% (approximately).

points.label: Improper Fractions
points.text: Numerator ≥ denominator. E.g., 7/4 (means 7 parts, but only 4 in a whole). Greater than or equal to 1.

points.label: Mixed Numbers
points.text: Whole number + fraction. 7/4 = 1¾ (one whole, plus ¾ more).

points.label: Conversion
points.text: 7÷4 = 1 remainder 3. So 7/4 = 1¾. Reverse: 1¾ = (1×4+3)/4 = 7/4.

example.problem: Convert 13/5 to a mixed number.

points.label: Same Denominator
points.text: ¼ + ¾ = (1+3)/4 = 4/4 = 1. Just add numerators.

points.label: Different Denominators
points.text: ½ + ⅓: Find common denominator (LCD). LCD(2,3)=6. ½=3/6, ⅓=2/6. 3/6+2/6=5/6.

points.label: Finding LCD
points.text: Multiples of 2: 2,4,6,8... Multiples of 3: 3,6,9... Least common = 6.

example.problem: A cricketer bats in 3 innings: scores ⅓, ¼, ⅕ of total runs. What fraction of total in all three?

points.label: Multiplication
points.text: ½ × ⅔ = (1×2)/(2×3) = 2/6 = ⅓. Numerator×numerator, denominator×denominator.

points.label: Division
points.text: ½ ÷ ⅔ = ½ × 3/2 = 3/4. Flip second fraction (reciprocal), then multiply.

points.label: Reciprocal
points.text: ⅔ flips to 3/2. Any fraction's reciprocal: swap numerator and denominator.

slides.title: The Tournament Results
slides.storyContext: Arjun practices daily. His average improves: 12 hits in 16 attempts → 12/16 = ¾ = 0.75 = 75%. He shows Priya his scorecard. 'You did it! You hit the pro's average!' Priya smiles. 'Now you understand: ¾, 0.75, 75%—they're the same champion.'

points.text: Fractions (¾), decimals (0.75), and percentages (75%) express the same value.
Convert by dividing (fraction→decimal) or using powers of 10 (decimal→fraction).
Simplify fractions using GCD to see the clearest form.
Some fractions repeat (⅓ = 0.333...), others terminate (¼ = 0.25).

subject: Science
title: Priya's Organic Farm in Punjab
hook: Priya's grandparents run an organic farm near Amritsar, Punjab. They grow wheat and rice using rotation, composting, and natural pest control. How do crop selection, soil quality, and water management make farming successful?

slides.title: Crop Production and Management: Farm Wisdom
Grandpa's Wheat Field
slides.storyContext: Priya visits the Punjab farm during harvest. Golden wheat fields stretch for acres. 'Grandpa, how do you keep this soil so rich year after year?' Baldev smiles: 'We rotate crops—wheat one year, legumes next. We compost, we let the land rest. The soil is living.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Good farming needs planning, soil care, and rotation.

image.alt: Grandpa's Wheat Field — Crop Production and Management

slides.title: The Soil Test
slides.storyContext: Priya and Grandpa Baldev dig into the black soil. 'See these worms and insects? They're farmers too—breaking down dead leaves, making nutrients available.' He crumbles a handful: 'This texture, this color—it took decades of organic practice to build. Chemical farming would have killed it.'

points.label: Nutrients (NPK)
points.text: Crops need Nitrogen (N), Phosphorus (P), Potassium (K). Ratios vary by crop. Wheat needs high N; legumes add N to soil.

points.label: Water Management
points.text: Irrigation timing is critical. Wheat in Punjab: rabi crop (winter); rice: kharif (monsoon). Wrong water timing = crop failure.

points.label: Light & Temperature
points.text: Wheat thrives in cool season. Rice in warm, monsoon season. Altitude and latitude affect crop choice.

points.label: Nitrogen (N) — The Leafy Nutrient
points.text: Makes plants green, promotes leaf & stem growth. Deficiency: pale leaves, stunted growth. Wheat & corn are hungry for N.

points.label: Phosphorus (P) — Root & Flower Builder
points.text: Aids root growth, flower & fruit development. Deficiency: weak roots, poor crops. Critical for legume pods.

points.label: Potassium (K) — Disease Fighter
points.text: Strengthens plant immunity, improves water retention. Deficiency: weak stems, disease-prone. Needed by fruits & tubers.

example.problem: Grandpa grows wheat (high N demand) year 1. What should he grow year 2 to restore nitrogen?
example.solution: Grow legumes (chickpea, peas, clover). They have nitrogen-fixing bacteria in roots that add N to soil. Year 3: wheat again, with richer soil.

image.alt: Example 1: Crop Rotation — Crop Production and Management

slides.title: Legumes to the Rescue
slides.storyContext: Year 2, Grandpa plants chickpeas where wheat grew. Priya asks: 'Why chickpeas after wheat?' He explains: 'Chickpeas have root nodules with special bacteria—they pull nitrogen from the air and lock it in the soil. Free fertilizer! In year 3, the soil is restored.'

points.label: Rabi (Winter) Crops
points.text: Wheat, mustard, peas planted Oct-Nov after monsoon. Need winter rain or canal irrigation. Harvest Feb-Mar.

points.label: Kharif (Monsoon) Crops
points.text: Rice, maize, cotton planted Jun-Jul when monsoon rains start. Heavy water needs from nature. Harvest Sep-Oct.

points.label: Zaid (Summer) Crops
points.text: Watermelon, cucumber, pumpkin planted Mar-Apr. Short season, needs irrigation. Harvest Jun-Jul.

points.label: Too Much Water
points.text: Waterlogging, root rot, fungal disease. Soil must drain well; fields need canals or drains.

points.label: Too Little Water
points.text: Drought stress, wilting, poor yield. Crops need consistent moisture, not flooding then dry.

points.label: Timing Matters
points.text: Wheat needs 4-5 irrigation cycles: Nov-Dec, Jan (tillering), Feb (boot), Mar (grain fill). Skip if winter rains are good.

example.problem: Grandpa grows rabi wheat planted Oct 15. Monsoon ends; soil moisture drops. When to irrigate?
example.solution: Wheat needs critical stages: Nov-Dec (if dry), Jan (tillering), Feb (boot stage), Mar (grain fill). Too early = waterlogging; too late = drought stress.

points.label: Tilling & Mulching
points.text: Loosen soil before planting (tilling). Mulch (straw, leaves) retains moisture, blocks weeds, prevents erosion.

points.label: Compost Making
points.text: Layer farm waste: dried leaves, crop residue, kitchen scraps. Add water, let decompose 3-6 months. Golden brown = ready.

points.label: Manure & Organic Matter
points.text: Cow/poultry manure is organic fertilizer. Improves soil texture, water-holding capacity, microbial activity.

example.problem: Grandpa has wheat straw, cow dung, and vegetable scraps. Make compost for next year's soil.
example.solution: Layer: straw (carbon) + cow dung (nitrogen + microbes) + water. Repeat layers. Turn every 2 weeks. In 4 months, dark crumbly compost. Mix 2-3 tons into soil before planting.

points.label: Beneficial Insects
points.text: Ladybugs eat aphids, parasitic wasps kill caterpillars, ground beetles eat slugs. Attract them with flowers (marigold, sunflower).

points.label: Neem & Organic Sprays
points.text: Neem oil (2% in water) targets aphids/mites without harming bees or microbes. Spray every 7-10 days during pest season.

points.label: Crop Rotation & Intercropping
points.text: Rotate crops to break pest cycles. Intercrop (maize+beans) confuses pests and maximizes space.

slides.title: Battle Against Aphids
slides.storyContext: Spring, and aphids swarm the young wheat. Grandpa spots them early. He walks to the field edge where marigolds bloom—they've attracted ladybugs. 'See? Ladybugs eat aphids. Nature's pest control. Free and harmless. No poison, no dead insects, just balance.'

example.problem: Grandpa notices aphids on wheat. Mix neem oil spray: 2% neem oil in water. Spray at sunrise. How often?
example.solution: Spray every 7-10 days during pest season. Repeat 3-4 times. Natural neem targets aphids without harming bees or soil microbes.

image.alt: Example 4: Neem Spray Application — Crop Production and Management

points.label: Hand Weeding
points.text: Pull weeds by hand (organic farms). Best after rain when soil is soft. Remove roots entirely to prevent regrowth.

points.label: Mulching
points.text: 2-3 inches of straw/leaves around plants prevents weed growth, retains moisture, regulates soil temperature.

points.label: Herbicide Risk
points.text: Chemical herbicides poison soil microbes and harm beneficial insects. Organic = manual + mulch + rotation.

points.label: Intercropping Example
points.text: Plant maize + beans together. Beans climb maize; maize shades soil. Both thrive; pests confused by mixed crop.

points.label: Companion Planting
points.text: Tomato + basil (pest control). Carrot + onion (pest control). Cucumber + marigold (attracts ladybugs).

points.label: Benefits
points.text: More yield per area, natural pest control, soil health, reduced pesticide need.

slides.title: Challenge 1: Design a Crop Rotation Plan

example.problem: Grandpa has 2 fields. Field A: wheat, Field B: needs a 3-year plan. What rotation works?
example.solution: Year 1: A-wheat, B-legume (chickpea). Year 2: A-legume, B-maize. Year 3: A-maize, B-wheat. Each field rests and gets legume nitrogen boost.

example.problem: Wheat field shows leaf-spot disease (fungal). Grandpa wants organic control. What three steps?
example.solution: 1) Remove & burn infected leaves (reduce disease source). 2) Spray sulfur powder or neem oil every 7 days. 3) Improve air circulation (thin weaker plants). Organic + targeted = saved crop.

example.problem: Rice crop (kharif) planted Jun 15. Monsoon rain is irregular. When to provide supplementary irrigation?
example.solution: Rice needs 5-7 cm water per week. Monitor: if 10 days pass without 5 cm rain, irrigate. Especially critical during grain-fill (Aug-Sep) when yield sets.

points.label: Clay Soil
points.text: Heavy, retains water (good), drains poorly (bad). Needs compost to improve drainage. Punjab's black soil is clay-rich.

points.label: Sandy Soil
points.text: Light, drains fast (good for waterlogging areas), doesn't retain nutrients (bad). Needs organic matter and frequent watering.

points.label: Loamy Soil
points.text: Best balance: clay + sand + silt. Retains moisture, drains well, holds nutrients. Ideal for most crops.

example.problem: Grandpa's field has heavy clay soil. How to improve it for better drainage and crop growth?
example.solution: Add 5-10 cm compost or sand + organic manure. Till to mix. Add straw mulch. In 2-3 seasons, soil becomes more loamy (better structure). Crop yields improve.

points.label: Quality Seeds
points.text: Use certified seeds: high purity, viability ≥80%, low moisture (8-12%). Store in cool, dry place.

points.label: Germination
points.text: Seeds need moisture, warmth, air. Dormant seeds wait for right conditions. Poor storage kills seeds.

points.label: Seed Rate
points.text: Amount of seed per unit area. Wheat: 125 kg/hectare. Too much = overcrowding; too little = sparse crop.

example.problem: Grandpa stores wheat seeds from this year's harvest for next season. Moisture: 12%. Where and how to store?
example.solution: Cool, dry, dark place (below 20°C, <60% humidity). Containers: jute bags or sealed drums. Check monthly for pests. Keep away from ammonia/fertilizer.

points.label: Prevention First
points.text: Rotation, clean seeds, resistant varieties, sanitation—prevent before treating.

points.label: Early Detection
points.text: Monitor crops weekly. Spot yellowing, spots, wilting, holes early. Act before spread.

points.label: Organic Arsenal
points.text: Neem, sulfur, Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis), ladybugs, yellow/blue traps, hand-pick large pests.

slides.title: Harvest Time & Lessons Learned
slides.storyContext: Harvest comes. Grandpa's wheat is golden, thick, disease-free. Priya helps gather the yield. 'Your rotation, compost, neem spray—they all worked!' Baldev nods: 'Yes. This is sustainable farming—we take from earth, we return to it. The soil stays alive for grandchildren.'

slides.title: Sustainable Farming

points.text: Crop rotation, composting, and natural pest control sustain soil health.
NPK nutrients, water timing, and seasonal crops must match.
Rabi (wheat, Oct-Mar), Kharif (rice, Jun-Sep), Zaid (summer vegetables).
Organic methods (neem, ladybugs, mulch) beat chemical pesticides—no poison, no dead soil.

slides.inSimpleWords: Respect soil, rotate crops, use nature wisely.

image.alt: Sustainable Farming — Crop Production and Management
